title: When Faith becomes something else
body:
When Faith Became Something Else

Sometimes we don’t walk away from God.
We walk away from what we thought God had become.

Maybe faith began to feel like obligation. Rules. Judgment. People telling us what we should believe or how we should live. Maybe we saw hypocrisy in people who spoke about God but seemed to have very little mercy for anyone around them.

And somewhere along the way, we stopped coming.

Today’s Gospel is worth hearing if that has ever been you.

Because Jesus saw it too.

He looked directly at the religious leaders of His time and said:

“You have neglected the weightier things of the law: judgment and mercy and fidelity.”

They were doing the religious things. They knew the rules. They observed the smallest requirements of the law.

But Jesus looked beneath all of it and asked: What happened to your heart?

That matters.

Because sometimes the very things that have caused people to turn away from religion are things Jesus Himself condemned.

Hypocrisy bothered Him.
Self-righteousness bothered Him.
Religion without mercy bothered Him.

He wasn’t asking people to abandon faith because of it. He was calling them back to what faith was supposed to be.

And perhaps He still is.

In the first reading, Paul speaks to people who are confused and unsettled. His words are simple: “Stand firm.” Don’t allow every voice, every disappointment, every frightening moment to separate you from what you once knew.

Maybe you aren’t standing very firmly right now.

Maybe you haven’t been inside a church for years. Maybe you’re not even certain what you believe anymore. Maybe something happened that made you decide you wanted nothing more to do with it.

But perhaps the fact that you are still wondering about God means the story isn’t finished.

Jesus never asked us simply to make the outside of the cup look clean. He wanted the inside transformed.

Mercy.
Faithfulness.
Justice.
Love.

This is the Christ who is still there beneath everything that may have disappointed you.

And maybe returning doesn’t begin with suddenly believing everything again. Maybe it begins much smaller.

A prayer you haven’t said in years.

Walking through the doors of a church and sitting quietly in the back.

Asking God one honest question:

“Are You still there?”

And perhaps His answer has been waiting all along:

I never left. Come and see.
